title: Windows Print Spooler and Print-Job Failures
exclusions: Detects two error records from the native `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin` channel: Event 372, which says a document failed to print and carries document, owner, printer, byte/page, client, and Win32-error context; and Event 808, which says the spooler failed to load a plug-in module and carries the module path, error code, and context value. The search does not claim that Event 372 means the Print Spooler service crashed, that the job never produced output, that every user-visible print failure emits 372, that an Event 808 module is malicious, or that a configured recovery action succeeded. It deliberately excludes informational Operational-channel Events 805 (rendering diagnostics) and 842 (print processor/driver-isolation context), successful Event 307 jobs, current queue depth, current service state, printer consumables, device hardware faults, print-server reachability, jobs on hosts whose Admin channel is absent, and failures overwritten before collection. It does not replace UC-1.2.4 for Service Control Manager failures of the `Spooler` service, establish root cause or adversary intent, prove estate-wide coverage, perform remediation, or provide regulatory assurance.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `UC-1.2.20 - Windows Print Spooler and Print-Job Failures` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, triggered rows, and dispositions; effective `[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin]` configuration and `btool` output; Windows, forwarder, and `Splunk_TA_windows` versions; expected-print-server inventory and source-health output; exact raw XML, `EventRecordID`, provider, channel, host, event/index times, and extracted Event 372 or 808 fields for every finding; the threshold approval; dashboard and alert-action revisions; any exact bounded exception; and dated positive, negative, boundary, extraction, duplicate, late-arrival, and recovery-context controls. For 372 preserve the document, owner, printer, data type, spool/printed bytes, total/printed pages, client, Win32 code, and rendered error text when present. For 808 preserve module path, hexadecimal error code, and context. These artifacts show what Windows recorded and what the documented search processed; this documentation-only review created no live Windows, print, Splunk, alert, or remediation evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Use an isolated index and absolute five-minute event-time bounds. Variant A contains three XML `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin` Event 372 records from provider `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService`, host `win-print-lab-01`, printer `Lab Queue A`, unique `EventRecordID` values, and `PrintOnProcFailedEd` values including `Param5=4096`, `Param6=0`, `Param7=1`, `Param8=0`, and `Param10=1722`; expect exactly one `print_job_failure_burst` row with `observed_events=3`, `threshold_events=3`, `threshold_window_minutes=5`, the three IDs, and extracted printer/error context. Variant B contains one Event 808 with `LoadPluginFailed.PluginDllName=C:\Windows\System32\spool\DRIVERS\x64\3\labplugin.dll` and `ErrorCode=0x7e`; expect exactly one `spooler_plugin_load_failure` row with `observed_events=1` and threshold one.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run independent variants and require zero rows: only two otherwise-valid Event 372 records for one host/printer in the closed five-minute window; three 372 records split across two printer identities; Events 805 and 842 from the Operational channel; Event 307 success; EventCode 372 from any provider other than `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService`; a 372 whose printer cannot be extracted; a valid event outside the absolute window; and a classic-rendered sample whose qualified source shape has not passed the deployment's extraction test. Confirm exact boundaries: two 372 records do not fire, three do; one 808 fires. A later successful 307 or current running `Spooler` state is recovery context and must not erase the historical error row.

dataSources: Primary source: the Windows Event Log `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin` channel and provider `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService`, collected locally from each in-scope print server by a supported Windows Universal Forwarder with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742). The preferred XML contract uses input `[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin]`, deployment-owned `index=wineventlog`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, and commonly `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin`; qualified historical deployments may instead expose `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin` or `sourcetype=WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin`. Required base fields are `_time`, `_indextime`, `_raw`, `host`, `source`, `sourcetype`, `EventCode`, `EventRecordID`, and provider. Event 372 XML `UserData/PrintOnProcFailedEd/Param1..Param11` carries document, owner, printer, data type, spool bytes, printed bytes, total pages, printed pages, client, Win32 code, and error text. Event 808 `UserData/LoadPluginFailed` carries `PluginDllName`, `ErrorCode`, and `Context`. This is event-driven collection, not a polled API; expected volume equals the error records Windows writes.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for the PrintService Admin-channel `WinEventLog` input and Windows Event Log parsing/search-time knowledge. Deploy collection configuration on supported Windows forwarders and the add-on's parsing/search knowledge on the Splunk tiers required by the topology. No premium Splunk app is required. The `wineventlog` index, saved search, thresholds, dashboard, exception register, and response workflow are deployment-owned content, not add-on defaults.
spl:
index=wineventlog earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m ((sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin") OR sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin" OR sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin") EventCode IN (372,808)
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID,event_id)), provider_name=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName,SourceName,EventSourceName), event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,'System.EventRecordID')
| where in(event_code,372,808) AND (provider_name="Microsoft-Windows-PrintService" OR match(_raw,"(?i)Provider Name=['\"]Microsoft-Windows-PrintService['\"]"))
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param1 output=document_name
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param2 output=document_owner
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param3 output=printer_name
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param4 output=data_type
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param5 output=spool_bytes_raw
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param6 output=printed_bytes_raw
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param7 output=total_pages_raw
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param8 output=printed_pages_raw
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param9 output=client_computer
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param10 output=win32_error_code
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param11 output=win32_error_text
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.LoadPluginFailed.PluginDllName output=plugin_module
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.LoadPluginFailed.ErrorCode output=plugin_error_code
| spath input=_raw path=Event.UserData.LoadPluginFailed.Context output=plugin_context
| eval document_name=coalesce(document_name,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param1'), document_owner=coalesce(document_owner,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param2'), printer_name=coalesce(printer_name,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param3'), data_type=coalesce(data_type,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param4'), spool_bytes=tonumber(coalesce(spool_bytes_raw,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param5')), printed_bytes=tonumber(coalesce(printed_bytes_raw,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param6')), total_pages=tonumber(coalesce(total_pages_raw,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param7')), printed_pages=tonumber(coalesce(printed_pages_raw,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param8')), client_computer=coalesce(client_computer,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param9'), win32_error_code=coalesce(win32_error_code,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param10'), win32_error_text=coalesce(win32_error_text,'PrintOnProcFailedEd.Param11'), plugin_module=coalesce(plugin_module,PluginDllName), plugin_error_code=coalesce(plugin_error_code,ErrorCode), plugin_context=coalesce(plugin_context,Context)
| eval issue_type=if(event_code=372,"print_job_failure_burst","spooler_plugin_load_failure"), entity=if(event_code=372,printer_name,plugin_module), error_code=if(event_code=372,win32_error_code,plugin_error_code), threshold_events=if(event_code=372,3,1), threshold_window_minutes=5
| where len(trim(entity))>0
| stats count as observed_events min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen max(_indextime) as last_indexed values(event_record_id) as event_record_ids latest(document_name) as document_name latest(document_owner) as document_owner latest(data_type) as data_type latest(spool_bytes) as spool_bytes latest(printed_bytes) as printed_bytes latest(total_pages) as total_pages latest(printed_pages) as printed_pages latest(client_computer) as client_computer latest(win32_error_text) as error_text latest(plugin_context) as plugin_context latest(_raw) as sample_raw by host event_code issue_type entity error_code threshold_events threshold_window_minutes source sourcetype
| where observed_events>=threshold_events
| eval unit="Windows error events per closed five-minute window", observation_semantics="historical_printservice_admin_error_not_current_queue_or_service_state", use_case="UC-1.2.20"
| table first_seen last_seen last_indexed host event_code issue_type entity error_code observed_events threshold_events threshold_window_minutes unit event_record_ids document_name document_owner data_type spool_bytes printed_bytes total_pages printed_pages client_computer error_text plugin_context source sourcetype observation_semantics use_case sample_raw
| sort 0 -last_seen host issue_type entity
description: Alerts on either three or more Microsoft PrintService Event 372 print-job failures for the same host and printer during one closed five-minute window, or any Event 808 spooler plug-in load failure. It preserves native byte, page, client, module, error, record, and source context while explicitly treating each row as historical Admin-channel evidence rather than current queue or service state.
value: Bursts of failed print jobs can interrupt shipping, labeling, clinical, finance, and office workflows, while a plug-in load failure can destabilize a shared print server or prevent driver-dependent queues from working. Separating documented error events from ordinary rendering and driver-isolation diagnostics gives responders earlier, lower-noise evidence and the exact Windows context needed to distinguish queue, network, driver, resource, and component problems.
implementation: Install and qualify `Splunk_TA_windows`, enable XML collection for `[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin]` into the governed Windows-event index, and verify provider, EventCode, EventRecordID, and UserData extraction on every supported Windows/add-on combination. Schedule the search every five minutes over the previous closed five-minute bucket. Trigger at three Event 372 records per host/printer or one Event 808 per host/module, throttle by `host,issue_type,entity`, and require responders to inspect the raw event, current queue and `Spooler` service state, printer/network reachability, and driver/component change history before declaring impact or changing the spooler.
visualization: Build a Windows printing-operations row with source health first: expected print servers missing recent Admin-channel telemetry; a newest-findings table showing host, issue type, printer or module entity, event/error code, event count versus threshold, first/last seen, native byte/page/client context, record IDs, and source age; a 24-hour timechart split by issue type; a host-by-printer heat map for repeated 372 bursts; and a module/error-code table for 808. Drill down to raw XML, the same printer's 307/372 history, same-time System/Application events, current queue and service checks, driver/change inventory, and the bounded exception record. Never display green current service or successful printing state solely because no row exists.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the primary rule. No single accelerated CIM dataset guarantees PrintService provider/channel identity, Event 372's eleven UserData values, Event 808's module/error/context values, or EventRecordID. The former `Change.All_Changes` query did not represent print-job or spooler plug-in failures and must not be used. At high print volume, summarize only after preserving host, event and index times, provider, channel, event code, EventRecordID, every native diagnostic field, source/sourcetype, threshold window, and raw-event drilldown, and after proving identical control-test results.

knownFalsePositives:
A result means Windows wrote the selected Admin-channel error. Here, a "false positive" means notification is expected, non-impacting, duplicated, or routed incorrectly; it does not mean ordinary CPU or backup activity can fabricate these event IDs.

1. **Event 372 despite physical output** — Microsoft-hosted examples show 372 can contain printed bytes equal to spool bytes, zero printed pages, and Win32 code `0` even when the page appeared. Compare `spool_bytes`, `printed_bytes`, page fields, error code/text, Event 307 history, the physical device or print-management record, and the user report. Keep the Windows error as evidence, but downgrade or close the incident when delivery is independently confirmed.

2. **Approved printer, driver, print-processor, port, or Point and Print change** — Queue recreation, OEM driver replacement, processor/port migration, and policy testing can generate 372 or 808. Match the exact host, printer/module, package/change ID, owner, and bounded UTC window. Preserve errors for change validation and suppress only notification for the exact entity.

3. **Printer or print network intentionally unavailable** — Device firmware work, address change, VLAN/firewall maintenance, or a paused queue can produce failed jobs. Confirm the device/change window and the native Win32 code; do not suppress other printers on the same server or extend the exception after the maintenance end.

4. **Controlled print load, failover, or NUL-port test** — Capacity tests and Microsoft-recommended queue-isolation troubleshooting can deliberately exercise spooling and failure paths. Use a lab queue where possible; otherwise identify the exact queue, test ID, expected event volume, and expiry, then retain the alert as test evidence.

5. **One user/application repeatedly retries one bad document** — A malformed spool stream, unsupported format, or application retry can cross the three-event threshold without a server-wide outage. Grouping by printer intentionally catches it; distinguish using document/client/owner fields and test another document, application, and queue. Route to the application or user owner rather than suppressing the printer globally.

6. **Automatic retry or successful recovery after the error** — A later Event 307, an empty queue, or a running `Spooler` service can show recovery. The original 372/808 remains genuine historical evidence. Use lifecycle logic to close or lower severity; never delete the error or infer recovery from elapsed time.

7. **Duplicate collection or replay** — Overlapping local and WEF inputs, cloned checkpoints, restored indexes, or routing duplication can repeat one `EventRecordID` and create an artificial burst. Compare record IDs, `_raw`, source, host, and `_indextime`; repair collection ownership rather than masking duplicates with broad `dedup`.

**Suppression contract:** if notification exceptions are permitted, use `windows_print_spooler_exceptions.csv` keyed by immutable asset identity plus exact `issue_type` and exact printer/module entity, with UTC `start_epoch`, UTC `end_epoch`, owner, approved change/test ID, and reason. Reject wildcards, host-only exceptions, duplicate keys, and non-expiring rows. Apply suppression after the primary measurement, publish suppressed rows separately, and never suppress source-health failures. The catalogue SPL intentionally has no lookup dependency, so an absent or malformed exception file cannot hide errors.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational PrintService error monitoring; no adversary behavior or malicious module is inferred)
detectionType: Native Windows error-event threshold and single-event fault detection
hardware: Supported Windows print servers or clients that host in-scope queues and expose the Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin channel. Physical printers, multifunction devices, print appliances, cloud print services, and third-party print-management products require their own telemetry for device, consumable, queue, and delivery state; this UC observes only Windows records on the collected host.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft PrintService Event 372, Event 808, spooler-state, and printing-troubleshooting documentation plus Splunk Windows Event Log, Splunk_TA_windows, source-type, and scheduled-alert documentation; input, XML extraction, fixtures, SPL, thresholds, dashboards, alerting, and response were specified but not executed on Windows, a printer, or a live Splunk platform; no Windows-version, add-on-version, Splunk-version, print-vendor, runtime, production, Microsoft, Splunk, or SME sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: Five-minute scheduled filtering of two sparse PrintService Admin-channel error IDs, deterministic XML extraction, one aggregation, and no joins, subsearches, real-time search, or data-model acceleration. Ingest depends on Admin-channel error volume.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact event contract

Assign a Windows print-platform owner, each business-critical queue's service owner, a Splunk collection/content owner, and a responder. Use supported Windows hosts with a qualified Universal Forwarder and Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows release. The collection identity needs local read access to Windows Event Log and normal forwarder transport; it does not require domain-administrator rights, queue administration, driver installation, spool-folder deletion, or permission to restart the `Spooler` service. The search role needs read access to the Windows-event index and permission to save/schedule the alert. Restrict raw job data because document names, owner names, client names, printer labels, and paths can expose personal or operational information.

Define the semantic boundary before collection. Microsoft Event 372 is a PrintService Admin-channel error whose message says a document failed to print and specifies eleven ordered values: document, owner, printer, data type, spool-file bytes, printed bytes, total pages, printed pages, client, Win32 error code, and rendered error text. Bytes are bytes and page values are counts; neither is a rate. Event 372 is not a spooler-crash event and does not guarantee that no physical output occurred. Microsoft documents causes including unreachable printers, resource pressure, invalid or incomplete spooler data, failed driver upgrades, and bad drivers. Event 808 says the print spooler failed to load a named plug-in module and supplies a hexadecimal Win32-style error code and context. A module-load error does not by itself prove malicious code.

The rule deliberately excludes Operational Event 805, which reports rendering diagnostics, and 842, which reports print processor/driver-isolation context. Those informational events can support investigation but are not failures merely because they exist. Event 307 is useful successful-job context. For service termination/start failures involving the service label `Print Spooler` or registry key `Spooler`, use UC-1.2.4 and verify current state; do not relabel 372 as a crash.

The Event 372 threshold is three records for the same host and printer in one closed five-minute bucket. Event 808 triggers at one record per host and module because Windows already classified the load operation as failed. These are catalogue starting points, not Microsoft or Splunk defaults. Approve them by print volume, retry behavior, business process, and response capacity. A low-volume label printer may need one 372; a high-volume shared queue may need a rate or failed-to-successful ratio after Event 307 coverage is validated. Keep units, window, grouping, and comparison explicit when tuning.

## Step 1 — Configure and qualify PrintService Admin collection

The PrintService Admin channel is the authoritative channel for both selected IDs. Do not point the rule at `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational`; that was the former UC's central source error. On each in-scope Windows print host, confirm in Event Viewer under Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > PrintService > Admin that the channel exists and records provider `Microsoft-Windows-PrintService`. Do not enable the high-volume Operational channel merely for this alert. If Operational data is enabled for troubleshooting or accounting, size and govern it separately.

Install `Splunk_TA_windows` according to the supported distributed topology. Never edit the add-on's `default` files. Put a reviewed stanza in `Splunk_TA_windows/local/inputs.conf` on the local Windows collection tier:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin]
disabled = 0
index = wineventlog
renderXml = 1
```

`index=wineventlog` is a deployment convention, not a reserved Splunk index. Create and secure it or replace the name consistently in inputs, SPL, roles, retention, dashboards, and tests. XML rendering preserves provider, channel, EventRecordID, event time, and structured UserData without depending on localized English message parsing. Deploy through configuration management and restart the forwarder when required. Verify effective precedence with `splunk btool inputs list WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin --debug`; confirm one owning app, XML rendering, enabled state, and intended index.

Current XML deployments commonly use `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and a channel-qualified source. Older add-on/platform combinations can use channel-qualified XML or classic source types. The catalogue SPL lists three accepted shapes for migration, but a production deployment should inspect raw events, retain only qualified branches, and fixture-test each accepted shape. Confirm `_time`, `_indextime`, host/originating computer, provider, EventCode, EventRecordID, source, sourcetype, and raw XML. For 372, verify `UserData/PrintOnProcFailedEd/Param1..Param11`; for 808, verify `UserData/LoadPluginFailed/PluginDllName`, `ErrorCode`, and `Context`. The SPL uses `spath` against raw XML and coalesces add-on extractions; it does not scrape localized rendered Message text.

Build independent source health. Compare the expected print-server inventory to `max(_time)` for the Admin channel, report missing hosts, measure `_indextime-_time`, and detect repeated `(host,EventRecordID)` values. Because this is an error channel, an idle host can legitimately have no recent selected IDs; source health must use any available Admin-channel events or a separately governed forwarder heartbeat and configuration inventory. Zero findings is not evidence that collection works.

## Step 2 — Create, understand, and schedule the search

Save the sidecar SPL as `UC-1.2.20 - Windows Print Spooler and Print-Job Failures`. Schedule it at `*/5 * * * *`, trigger when result count is greater than zero, and keep `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`. These bounds select one completed five-minute bucket with a five-minute indexing allowance and no event-time overlap. Measure p95/p99 delay and change delay/window together when needed. If events arrive later than five minutes, implement a tested late-arrival recovery search keyed by host and EventRecordID rather than widening overlapping windows and repeatedly paging old failures.

### Understanding this SPL

The base search constrains index, source shape, closed time, and Events 372/808. Numeric event-code normalization prevents string comparison surprises. Exact provider filtering rejects reused event numbers from other providers; the narrow raw-provider fallback exists for extraction failures and must be fixture-tested. `spath` reads documented XML paths. `coalesce` accepts equivalent add-on-extracted names, while `tonumber` ensures bytes/pages are numeric rather than lexical strings.

`issue_type` separates a 372 burst from an 808 component-load failure. For 372, `entity` is the printer name and the threshold is three; for 808, entity is the plug-in module and the threshold is one. Empty entities fail closed because grouping all unknown printers or modules would combine unrelated failures. `stats` creates one host/event/entity row for the closed bucket and retains first/last event times, latest indexing time, all record IDs, latest native context, and a raw example. `where observed_events>=threshold_events` is the only alert threshold. Final fields state the unit and historical observation semantics so downstream tickets do not call this current queue or service state.

Throttle notification by `host,issue_type,entity` for 30 minutes or let the incident platform own deduplication; retain every scheduled result for trend and evidence. Include observed count, threshold/window, event/error code, record IDs, and raw drilldown in the alert. Do not throttle all printers on a host together. If policy requires per-queue criticality and owner, enrich after measurement with an exact reviewed inventory; absent policy must produce a governance report, not silently redefine the native event.

There is no valid `Change.All_Changes` substitute. Print-job failure and plug-in UserData are not guaranteed by one CIM dataset. Keep the raw-event rule authoritative unless a governed summary preserves the complete contract and passes identical controls.

## Step 3 — Validate Windows semantics, XML extraction, and thresholds

First run the `controlTest` variants with fixed absolute times. Variant A must yield one 372 row only at the third same-printer event; assert every native field and three unique EventRecordIDs. Split the records across two printer names and require no row. Variant B must yield one 808 row from one event with exact module and error code. Test two versus three 372 records, one 808, an empty entity, nonnumeric byte/page values, duplicate IDs, another provider using 372, classic rendering, and late arrival. Preserve fixture, query revision, dispatch time, and output.

On a non-production Windows print server, compare raw Splunk XML to Event Viewer > Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > PrintService > Admin > Details > XML. Match provider, channel, Event ID, EventRecordID, computer, UTC time, and every UserData value. Use a benign lab queue and document that some failures can still produce output. A safe 372 exercise can use an isolated queue/device unavailable by approved design; do not disrupt a production shipping, prescription, identity-card, or finance printer. For 808, prefer an existing naturally occurring lab event or approved package/driver test; do not install an untrusted DLL or weaken Point and Print policy merely to generate telemetry.

Corroborate each finding at response time. Check the queue, print a controlled test page where safe, inspect successful Event 307 context, query `Get-Service -Name Spooler`, inspect same-time System/Application events, and review driver, print processor, port, network, firewall, firmware, and change records. Demonstrate that historical error, current service state, queue state, and physical output can disagree. This prevents the dashboard from presenting a past error as current outage.

Validate source coverage and latency across every supported Windows/add-on family. Confirm channel retention can survive the expected forwarder outage and that sensitive fields are access-controlled. This editorial review did not configure a forwarder, print a document, load a module, execute SPL, inspect a dashboard, or verify production thresholds. Keep `status=draft` until accountable Windows, print, and Splunk owners complete runtime qualification.

## Step 4 — Operationalize response, dashboards, exceptions, and evidence

Implement the dashboard described in `visualization` with source health first, a 24-hour operational range, and a seven- or thirty-day engineering trend range. Separate 372 and 808 panels because they have different entities and response paths. Show source age, threshold/window, and exception state beside findings. Restrict raw document/user/client fields to authorized operations staff; publish aggregated counts when broader audiences do not need those identifiers.

For a 372 burst, responders should verify raw fields and delivery report; determine whether one document/client/user or many are affected; test another document, application, queue, and printer; check queue pause/offline state, network reachability, port, device status, print processor and driver; inspect spool-folder health under an approved runbook; and correlate resource, firewall, firmware, deployment, and change context. For 808, identify the exact module, architecture, signer/package provenance, error code, driver/processor/monitor ownership, recent installation or policy change, and whether dependent queues fail. Escalate unknown or unapproved modules to security triage without claiming maliciousness from the event alone.

Do not automatically restart the spooler, clear `%WINDIR%\System32\spool\PRINTERS`, delete `.SPL`/`.SHD` files, remove drivers, change Point and Print restrictions, disable endpoint protection, edit print registry keys, or reboot from this alert. Microsoft troubleshooting includes some of those actions, but they require diagnosis, backup/change control, and business-impact review. Restarting or deleting files can destroy evidence and every hosted queue's work. Prefer reversible queue isolation and vendor-supported driver remediation.

Use only exact expiring notification exceptions described in `knownFalsePositives`. Preserve suppressed rows and source health. Retain the artifacts listed in `evidence`, including effective input, raw XML, threshold approval, controls, and disposition. A screenshot alone cannot prove what was collected or which search revision ran. Review extraction, thresholds, inventory, retention, runbooks, and access after Windows, add-on, driver, print-management, or topology changes.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot specific failures

- **No Admin-channel events:** confirm the channel exists in Event Viewer, the forwarder has the deployment app, the exact channel stanza is enabled, the index exists, output queues are healthy, and local retention has not overwritten records. Use `btool --debug` to find a higher-precedence disabled or misrouted stanza.
- **Only Operational 805/842 events arrive:** collection targets the wrong channel. Add the Admin stanza and keep Operational accounting/troubleshooting data separate; do not reinterpret informational diagnostics as failure.
- **Provider, EventRecordID, or UserData fields are null:** verify XML rendering and intact raw XML, add-on knowledge on the search tier, and actual source shape. Compare Event Viewer XML. Do not replace structured extraction with English Message regex.
- **372 rows never reach three:** inspect printer extraction, exact identity variation, schedule bounds, event latency, and user retry behavior. Tune only with measured queue volume and impact; do not combine all printers to force a result.
- **372 fires although output appeared:** compare bytes/pages, code/text, Event 307, device/accounting record, and user confirmation. This is a documented semantic limitation, not proof the SPL is wrong.
- **808 module is `unextracted` or missing:** inspect `LoadPluginFailed` raw XML and namespace/path on that Windows version. Fail closed, update fixtures and extraction deliberately, and never group all missing modules.
- **Repeated record IDs inflate count:** locate duplicate local/WEF routes, cloned checkpoints, restore/replay, or routing overlap. Repair the source; do not hide the defect with unconditional `dedup` because repeated IDs are evidence of telemetry quality failure.
- **Alerts arrive late:** measure `_indextime-_time`, clock synchronization, forwarder queues, and channel retention. Move the closed-bucket delay from measured evidence and add a keyed late-arrival path if required.
- **`Spooler` is stopped but this search is quiet:** expected when no 372/808 was recorded. Use Service Control Manager events/current-state checks and UC-1.2.4; this rule is not a service heartbeat.
- **CIM/tstats gives different results:** expected. Return to raw PrintService Admin events unless a separately governed normalization proves complete field and count parity.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for Windows reports that several documents failed on the same printer or that the printing service could not load one of its parts. The team then checks the printer, queue, network, and software before important printing work is interrupted.
